title: Question 7
stem:
A varying current I passes through a resistor of resistance R in the circuit shown in Fig. 7.1.
Fig. 7.2 shows the variation with time t of I.
The current has magnitude 2I_{0}when it is in the positive direction and I_{0} when it is in the negative
direction. The period of the variation of the current is T.

parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 7.2 for the size of the current when it is below the time axis, and remember that heating does not depend on which way charge flows.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Power Depends on Current Squared**
You know that a resistor always dissipates energy as heat whenever current flows, whichever direction it flows. That is because power is proportional to the square of the current, so a minus sign disappears on squaring.

Step 2: **Insert the Negative-Direction Magnitude**
From Fig. 7.2 the magnitude in the negative direction is $I_0$. So: $$P = I^2 R = (-I_0)^2 R = I_0^2 R$$

walkthrough:

Step 2: **Square the Full Value**
$$P = I^2 R = (2I_0)^2 R = 4I_0^2 R$$ Doubling the current gives four times the power.

markscheme_points.text: sketch: square wave of period $T$, with $P$ always non-zero
horizontal lines, from 0 to $0.5T$ and from $1.0T$ to $1.5T$, all at the same level that the scale indicates to be $I_0^2 R$

hints: Hint 1: Think about whether $P$ can ever be negative or zero here, given that current is always flowing in one direction or the other.
Hint 2: Link each time interval in Fig. 7.2 to your two power values from part (a), noting when the current switches at $0.5T$, $1.0T$ and $1.5T$.
Hint 3: Compare the heights of the two levels on your $P$ axis and decide how to label them so the upper level is clearly four times the lower level.
parts.proper_answer: Square wave of period $T$ with $P > 0$ at all times. $P = I_0^2 R$ from $0$ to $0.5T$ and $1.0T$ to $1.5T$; $P = 4I_0^2 R$ from $0.5T$ to $1.0T$ and $1.5T$ to $2.0T$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Shape Is Still Square but All Positive**
Current jumps sharply between constant values, so power also jumps sharply between constant values. And because $P = I^2R$, power stays positive even when $I$ is negative. So you draw horizontal lines, never going to zero.

Step 2: **Place the Lower and Upper Levels**
From $t = 0$ to $0.5T$, $I = -I_0$ so $P = I_0^2R$. Draw a horizontal line at that low level. From $t = 0.5T$ to $1.0T$, $I = +2I_0$ so $P = 4I_0^2R$. Draw a horizontal line four times higher. Repeat the pattern: low from $1.0T$ to $1.5T$, high from $1.5T$ to $2.0T$.

Step 3: **Label the Power Axis**
Mark the lower level as $I_0^2R$ and the upper level as $4I_0^2R$ on the $P$ axis. The pattern repeats every $T$, giving two full cycles between $0$ and $2.0T$.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on one full period $T$, where the low power and high power each act for exactly half the time, and think about how to average the two levels.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Average Over One Period**
Mean power is the total energy per period divided by the period. In time $T$, low power $I_0^2R$ acts for $T/2$ and high power $4I_0^2R$ acts for $T/2$.

Step 2: **Calculate the Average**
$$\langle P \rangle = \frac{1}{2}I_0^2R + \frac{1}{2}(4I_0^2R) = \frac{5}{2}I_0^2R$$ This is the constant power level that would give the same area under the $P$-$t$ graph.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall that $I_{r.m.s.}$ is defined as the steady DC current that would dissipate the same mean power in the same resistor $R$.
Hint 2: Set the DC power expression equal to your mean power from (c)(i) and solve for $I_{r.m.s.}$ in terms of $I_0$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Mean Power to R.M.S. Current**
By definition, a DC current equal to $I_{r.m.s.}$ through $R$ gives the same heating as the varying current. So: $$\langle P \rangle = I_{r.m.s.}^2 R$$

Step 2: **Equate and Solve**
Insert the result from (c)(i): $$I_{r.m.s.}^2 R = \frac{5}{2}I_0^2 R$$ Cancel $R$ and take the square root: $$I_{r.m.s.} = \sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}I_0$$
